Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. The jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization’s board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater. Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. “Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. “Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid. WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city manager Under cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms’ niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time. “You knew they were city employees,” Murrell said. “And it bothered you that they were doing this?” Murrell said. “I thought it was a little odd,” Cox said. “You didn’t raise any objections,” Murrell said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney’s presence at the meetings. “He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?” Murrell said. “He didn’t raise any objections or concerns, did he?” Murrell said. “Not at the meeting,” Cox said. Not that I know of,” Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

Eight months after a Port St. Lucie father vanished, his family says they are still searching for answers and living with the painful uncertainty of not knowing where he is. "I'm stuck in this cycle of not knowing where he is," said Aubrey Finley, whose brother, Robert La Polla , disappeared Jan. 8 after being released from a hospital in Fort Pierce. The 47-year-old father has not been seen or heard from since, according to his family. Detectives have no confirmed sightings, and the case remains unsolved. Finley said La Polla struggled with depression following the deaths of their parents, but the siblings remained close and talked often. "Everything kind of fell apart," she said. "But we still managed to communicate a lot. We were still there for each other all the time." Also read: Search underway for missing autistic man last seen at Jensen Beach home Thursday morning Because of that bond, Finley said her brother's disappearance is completely out of character. In the months since he vanished, family members and friends have organized search efforts across Fort Pierce, checking wooded areas and busy corridors near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. "We've gone through woods, under bridges, talking to people everywhere in Fort Pierce, trying to find anything that brings us to him," Finley said. The search has also taken an emotional toll on La Polla's young daughter, who continues to wait for her father to come home. She misses him," Finley said. "He's got a family that love him." The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office (SLCSO) said La Polla has been entered into a national missing persons database. Investigators have also collected DNA from family members in case it is needed for identification and continue to follow up on leads. Anyone with information about La Polla's whereabouts is asked to contact Detective Cpl. Drawdy at 772-462-3230 or call 911.

A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms is on trial over allegations that he improperly influenced a city bidding process involving two vacant lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. Mimms faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors allege he steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included Mimms' niece and another city employee. On Thursday, much of the testimony focused on who controlled the RFP process and how closely Mimms remained involved after it was turned over to the city's purchasing department. FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails and other records collected during the investigation. One focus was the nearby Lincoln Theater and its need for parking. Brisky testified Mimms had told the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency that the RFP would include language addressing the theater's parking needs. But that language was not included in the request Mimms sent to the purchasing department. Brisky also testified investigators found no evidence Mimms filed a 2019 memorandum concerning the parking plans in the relevant city records. The defense questioned the significance of that omission and emphasized that the purchasing department was responsible for putting together and publishing the RFP after receiving the project's specifications. See also: NTSB report clarifies Amazon plane crash timeline that killed 5 on Sept. 6 Defense attorneys also challenged the state's characterization of the process as a sole-source arrangement. Brisky acknowledged the RFP was not technically a sole-source contract. The state, meanwhile, pointed to emails showing Mimms continued to communicate with city employees about the RFP, including its evaluation criteria and the evaluation committee. Other emails showed city employees knew there had been one submission after the RFP was posted. An LPYP email address was copied on one of those communications. The defense also questioned the investigation's treatment of other city employees involved in the process, including a purchasing official who was not charged. Later, former Fort Pierce employee Kalita Scott testified about LPYP and its efforts to develop the Lincoln Park properties. She described the organization as a group of young professionals focused on community development and said the need for parking near the Lincoln Theater was known in the community. Prosecutors allege Mimms manipulated the city's process to ensure LPYP received the lease. A new school designed specifically for neurodivergent children has opened in Palm Beach Gardens, bringing education and therapy services together under one roof. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance both hit the campaign trail on Thursday, but headed to heavily Republican areas to shore up lagging enthusiasm in their party ahead of next month’s midterm elections.Trump’s travel to Texas and Oklahoma kicked off what the president said will be a 32-day campaign blitz leading up to Nov. 3.“I think we’re going to win. Every place I’ve gone, we win,” Trump said during a speech at a truck facility in Denton, northwest of Dallas. He said some have suggested his “heart isn't in it. My heart is in it,” and if not, he'd promised he'd be “home right now.”“My heart is in it like never before,” Trump said of the run-up to the midterms.Vance, meanwhile, stumped in Florida, putting the Republican Party’s highest-ranking officials in areas where GOP candidates once expected to have glide paths to victory but are now facing tougher races.The vice president tried to cast the GOP as representing common sense in the face of a Democratic push to the left.“I have the easiest job in the world,” the vice president said in Lakeland, Florida. “I get to talk about how crazy the Democrats are.”RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground statesTrump and Vance could have their work cut out for them, though.A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.Republicans have expressed growing pessimism about their chances in the election, which will determine control of Congress, as the president has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.According to Trump, his party has merely done a poor job of public relations in promoting his administration's accomplishments.“Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it,” Trump said in Texas.Still, the president spent far more time scoffing at his predecessor, President Joe Biden, reliving his 2024 presidential campaign and defending the war in Iran than he did talking about how he'll help lower the cost of living.Trump scoffed at questions about affordability, insisting that they'd been caused by Biden, who left office more than two years ago. He also insisted that prices were actually on the decline.“I think inflation is very real, but they’re the ones that caused the inflation,” he said. “I’m the one that’s bringing it down, and we have to be able to get that word out somehow because they’re using the word affordability.”Democrats say Trump is desperateThe Democratic National Committee said Trump and Vance are “desperately trying to rally their base as the midterm elections approach and Republicans face defeat.”“Donald Trump and JD Vance started a deadly and costly war with Iran that sent the economy spiraling and pushed prices even higher, and now — in the final stretch to the midterms — they’re desperately pleading with voters to 'give (them) another chance,'” said DNC deputy communications director Kendall Witmer.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'Pretend that I'm on the ballot': Trump courts Republicans at unusual GOP midterm conventionIn Oklahoma, Trump campaigned with Republican Mike Mazzei, who is running against Democratic state House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson for governor. That event was held on the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, putting Trump in the company of just a handful of U.S. presidents who have visited tribal nations while in office.Before his evening Oklahoma stop, Trump toured the truck facility and chatted with workers in Texas, where Republicans are spending heavily to try to bolster state Attorney General Ken Paxton in a Senate race that could be closer than long expected. Paxton is facing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico,Paxton attended the event and Trump joked that he “could be a pain in the ass sometimes” but also noted, “We need Ken so badly, and that’s why I’m here.”Trump didn't summon Paxton to the stage. He also shouted out, but didn't invite to speak, an unlikely traveler accompanying him, former NBA star Dennis Rodman. Trump praised Rodman as his longtime friend and said Rodman had become close with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.Trump promises a travel blitz coming upThe president will be campaigning in more politically competitive areas in the weeks ahead as he embarks on his travel sprint. But Republican officials will not send him to places where they think his presence could drag down their candidates, according to a person familiar with the party’s strategy who was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.Trump’s Oklahoma visit, and likewise one on Friday to Alabama, aimed at hitting two targets with one stop, the person said.Republican officials have noted that even his Oklahoma stop brought Trump close to the Dallas-Fort Worth media market, meaning the president's message reached Texas voters who could back Paxton.His Friday stop in Mobile, Alabama, is aimed not only at boosting Sen. Tommy Tuberville as he runs for Alabama governor but also at shoring up support in Florida’s adjacent panhandle for Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.Donalds is running for Florida governor against David Jolly, the Republican-turned-independent who is now running as a Democrat. Donalds' campaign in heavily GOP Florida comes as Republicans there have faced some turbulence and voter concerns about affordability and artificial intelligence data centers have become central issues.With Trump in Oklahoma and Texas, Vance's central Florida stop on Thursday was for Donalds. That came a day after the vice president campaigned in Texas, rallying with Republican candidate Eric Flores, who is in a tight U.S. House race in south Texas.Trump will also campaign on Saturday in Vandalia, Ohio, and on Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska.Trump is expected to campaign for the GOP almost dailyIn a meeting on Capitol Hill this week, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles described privately to GOP senators that Trump will have a near-daily sprint of campaigning ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito said that White House officials are “acknowledging the headwinds” but that “they have a strategy, and we have a strategy,” including money that the president’s operation will continue to deploy.Capito also defended the White House’s plan to send Trump to traditionally conservative territory, arguing that he can motivate the Republican base not just where he travels but elsewhere in the country because he has such a broad reach.“He can get more of his voters out — that are going to be our voters — than anybody else,” Capito said.

It's hard to find the guys with that kind of role acceptance and still be really good at at those things," Spoelstra said.Davion Mitchell: 'Off Night' is learning from the bestDavion Mitchell or "Off Night," as some call him, is another guard who could play a pivotal role in Miami's success. So little things like that," Mitchell said.Beyond Wiggins and Mitchell, Miami also returns guards Pelle Larsson and Drew Smith. Guys coming in like that, it just make the whole training camp just a lot better," Mitchell said.Miami's first preseason game is Saturday against the Toronto Raptors. The regular season begins Oct.

Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in two separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. According to an arrest affidavit, 23-year-old Giovanny Barthelemy was driving a silver Toyota Highlander around 8:40 p.m. Tuesday when it collided with a 16-year-old riding an electric motorcycle on Southwest Roma Way near Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at the community clubhouse recorded the crash. The officer wrote that the video shows the SUV turning into the community entrance as the teen crossed in front of it. The teen was thrown from the motorcycle. The affidavit says the SUV then backed up and drove away while the injured teen lay on the ground waving his arms. The teen was taken to Tradition Medical Center and then flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said he broke his left femur and hurt his left ankle, and he was listed in serious but stable condition. See also: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges, enters not guilty plea One witness told police the electric motorcycle had no headlights. Two witnesses said both vehicles were going fast. The SUV's owner, the father of Barthelemy's girlfriend, called 911. He told police Barthelemy said he had hit someone on a bike and then driven home. Officers found Barthelemy at his home on Southwest Ridgecrest Drive. According to the affidavit, after being read his rights, Barthelemy told police he felt and heard the crash and knew right away he had hit a person. He told police he should have stopped but didn't, and said his phone was dead, according to the affidavit. Barthelemy is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries, which is a felony. He was also given a traffic citation. He was released on a $7,500 bond. The second case happened earlier that afternoon. Lucie officer clocked a silver Toyota going 85 mph in a 40-mph zone, according to an arrest affidavit. The officer turned around and tried to stop the car. The affidavit says the driver went over a concrete median into the opposite lanes, ran a red light, and hit a traffic sign at Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street before getting on northbound Interstate 95. The officer turned off his lights and siren but kept the car in sight. Police said the car later broke down on the side of I-95. Officers said the driver, 19-year-old Christian Johnson, got out and ran toward the back of the car. Lucie detective, a Florida Highway Patrol trooper, and the officer surrounded the car, and Johnson was taken into custody. According to the affidavit, Johnson's license had been suspended three times in St. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving and driving with a suspended or revoked license. All three charges are misdemeanors. He was released on a $12,500 bond. In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

WPTV learned there are 13 license plate reader cameras in St. Lucie County that don't have permits, according to county staff.Wednesday, Sept. 30, was the deadline the Florida Department of Transportation gave municipalities to remove the license plate readers from state-controlled roads.WATCH BELOW: Unpermitted license plate readers found in St. Lucie CountyNow WPTV is pressing city leaders about why the cameras are there, who they belong to, and what is happening to the cameras now.On Thursday, WPTV spoke to Ricky Mathura, who works at a gas station off Orange Avenue and 25th Street in Fort Pierce, where one of the unpermitted license plate readers was found."I don't know why it's there," said Mathura. Lucie County Communications Director Erick Gill said they're trying to find that out."We don't know who they belong to," Gill said. "They were just put in our right-of-way."The county says there's 53 permitted license plate readers on their right-of-ways and gave WPTV a list with all the locations of the unpermitted license plate readers staff found.RELATED: FDOT revokes permits for automated license plate readers"We were surprised, you know, that were that many out there,” said Gill.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office told WPTV they claimed three of them but are working to find out why they weren't permitted.Gill said county staff is actively working to identify the owners of the other readers and taped notices on the cameras for the owners to take them down within 30 days.Once the 30 days are up, Gill said staff will remove the readers safely."We'll begin the process of either removing them if we feel like we can safely remove them without damaging the equipment and endangering our staff, or at least covering up so the cameras can't capture any surveillance," Gill said.

The Florida Department of Health in Martin County is informing residents that several sentinel chickens have tested positive for West Nile virus.The department and Martin County Mosquito Control said they are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases, as well as targeted mosquito treatment to reduce the risk of disease transmission.Individuals with symptoms of fever, chills, sweats, nausea/vomiting, and headache should seek immediate medical attention, the department said.The health department is reminding the community to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking these basic precautions:Spray yourself with mosquito repellentCover your arms and legs with clothingDrain standing waterMosquitoes breed by laying eggs in and near standing water and as little as one bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to multiply, the health department said.For more information, click here.

As Jupiter Fire Rescue officially began its first day on Thursday, one of the department’s new firefighters is already being recognized for the life-saving work she does.At a recent Jupiter Town Council meeting, Jessica Herman was honored for her heroic actions that helped save a retired NYPD officer who went into cardiac arrest.WATCH: Jupiter Firefighter Honored for Lifesaving RescueJupiter Fire Rescue Deputy Chief Jason Sekula read a letter to Herman before she was given the Phoenix Life Saving Award."Although you recently joined JFRD, you demonstrated the character, leadership, and heart of a veteran firefighter," Sekula said.Herman was at a first responders tournament in Coral Springs on 9/11 when Joe Gomes felt something was off. "I just got this odd feeling over my entire body, and to myself, I said, 'that feels weird,'" Gomes said.He lay down and was able to walk off the ice on his own, but within seconds, his teammates realized this was an emergency.Herman ran toward Gomes, whom she'd known since he used to referee her junior hockey games. "I checked your pulse," Herman recalled. "I said, 'I don't have a pulse."She coordinated a team of six firefighters from different South Florida fire rescue departments to save Gomes. They're doing that, and we just got to work," Herman said.She began CPR compressions, and an AED defibrillator was brought out. "At one point, the bright white light came out," Gomes told WPTV.Herman said this was a true team effort. "I'm very humbled, and I'm extremely grateful for all the attention it's bringing. I keep reminding people I wasn't the only one," Herman said.Gomes says the experience left him with a new mission — making sure others are as lucky as he was that day. "There should be someone at all times working at the rink that knows CPR," he said.Now, Herman is bringing that same readiness to Jupiter as the town's new fire department starts its first day.

CROS Ministries seeks volunteers as demand for senior meal deliveries grows. CROS Ministries says its Caring Kitchen program has reached capacity serving seniors and homebound residents in the Delray Beach area, and now the nonprofit is looking for more volunteers as it works to expand.WATCH BELOW: Senior meal program at capacity, volunteers neededThe organization currently delivers about 2,000 healthy meals each month through its Caring Kitchen program. But with more people seeking help, leaders say they're no longer able to take on every new client."Right now we are at our maximum of 120 clients that we serve in this homebound meal deliveries," said Shona Castillo, Caring Kitchen program director. "I have a waitlist."The free meal delivery program serves seniors and homebound residents in Delray Beach and parts of Boca Raton. Volunteers help prepare, package and deliver meals directly to people who may otherwise struggle to access healthy food."I am looking for volunteers to help us deliver the meals to our seniors and our homebound," Castillo said.According to Castillo, inquiries for the service continue to come in.The nonprofit is now hoping to grow the program from roughly 120 to 150 clients in the coming months, but volunteers will be key to making that happen.Volunteer John Gavin has been delivering meals through the program for about a year and a half. On a recent route, he loaded freshly prepared meals and made deliveries to dozens of clients."We have 34 clients on this route," Gavin said. "It is a free service, and it's homemade food packed daily, it was made this morning fresh, packed, and it's to them before noon every day, Mondays and Wednesdays."Gavin said the growing need is evident."Definitely. And that's why I like working here. Almost every week I'm filling out a new application for someone," he said.While the organization is looking for more volunteers, Gavin said the experience can be rewarding for those who choose to help."The gift that I get from what I do here is something you can't pay for, and you don't realize that until you're involved doing this," Gavin said. "I get way more out of this than I'm putting into it."He added, "Having more volunteers is certainly something the Caring Kitchen could use, and it's rewarding. You wouldn't know it until you did it."For people who receive the meals, the service helps relieve financial pressure while ensuring access to nutritious food.Lyn Greenblatt, who has been receiving meals for several months, said the rising cost of living has gotten difficult."I'm on Social Security," Greenblatt said. "I have to pay partial rent with that and health insurance, which, you know, it's costly, so, yeah, it's tight."Without the deliveries, she said, "I'd probably make pasta and just live off of that because it's filling and easy to make."Greenblatt said the meals provide far more than just convenience."It's also balanced," she said. "There's a vegetable and a meal and maybe some pasta and a, it's always a vegetable. So, it's balanced."The deliveries also provide valuable social interaction."It's a visit too. It's not just a food delivery," Greenblatt said of Gavin. "He makes me feel comfortable."She added that having reliable meals available eases some of the stress that comes with living on a limited income."It's a very big stress relief because they're balanced, and I look forward to that," Greenblatt said.Castillo said the program receives food through food-recovery partnerships with organizations including the Palm Beach County Food Bank, Whole Foods and Publix. The group also purchases some food to accommodate special dietary needs, including meals for people with diabetes and other health conditions.The meals are prepared using USDA My Healthy Plate guidelines and are designed to provide nutritional value many recipients might otherwise miss."Most of them, because they're such a limited and tight budget, oftentimes they say they go to the Dollar Tree and they would normally just exist on tuna and crackers," Castillo said. "Our meals provide them that nutritional value that they are not receiving."Caring Kitchen volunteers are needed for meal preparation, packaging and deliveries. The program delivers meals on Mondays and Wednesdays.Caring Kitchen has been serving the Delray Beach community since 1993.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

According to the Florida Department of Children and Families, Florida is on pace to set a record for child drowning deaths. Drowning remains the leading cause of unintentional death for children ages 1 to 4.At the Infant Swimming Resource Swim School in Royal Palm Beach, instructors are teaching young children lifesaving skills that could make a difference in an emergency.WATCH BELOW: Parents seek water safety lessons with rising child drowning deaths"If your child falls into the water, they have one shot to roll and float to save themselves," said certified Infant Swimming Resource instructor Toni Ann Capanelli.For some children, learning those skills begins at a very young age. One 6-month-old recently experienced his first day of lessons. Instructors say it's normal for toddlers to cry as they adjust to being in the water."There is no discrimination. Any child can learn how to do this," Capanelli said.The Infant Swimming Resource program focuses on teaching children what instructors describe as survival skills. If a child unexpectedly enters the water, they are trained to roll onto their back, float, breathe and wait for help.The training typically takes six to eight weeks to complete, but instructors say the lessons do not end there. As children grow, their skills need adjustment and reinforcement through ongoing maintenance sessions."As their body grows, we need to adjust their roll and float," Capanelli said. "We set them up for a once-a-month maintenance lesson."For parents Shawn and Jill Kahn, enrolling their 14-month-old child in swim lessons was an easy choice."We are always fishing and boating and always by pools," one parent said. "It's really important that he learns how to swim, but I never learned how to swim."Cost can sometimes be a barrier for families, but instructors say financial assistance is available."ISR offers its own scholarships for families who need financial aid, and there are government programs," Capanelli said.For Capanelli, every child drowning serves as a reminder of why water safety education is so important."Drowning is preventable," she said. "I just wish that people understood how important it is to get your child's survival lessons, especially here in South Florida."Instructors also recommend brightly colored or neon swimwear for children, saying those colors can make it easier to spot a child in the water. They also remind parents that supervision is key.

Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. The jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization’s board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater. Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. “Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. “Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid. WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city manager Under cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms’ niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time. “You knew they were city employees,” Murrell said. “And it bothered you that they were doing this?” Murrell said. “I thought it was a little odd,” Cox said. “You didn’t raise any objections,” Murrell said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney’s presence at the meetings. “He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?” Murrell said. “He didn’t raise any objections or concerns, did he?” Murrell said. “Not at the meeting,” Cox said. Not that I know of,” Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

Florida's deadline to remove Flock cameras from highway rights-of-way is Wednesday, Sept. Lucie is also removing 18 cameras from city streets after pausing its program due to privacy concerns. Florida’s Department of Transportation mandated that local agencies remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by today. These cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. However, the state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Lucie, the city commission voted to have the vendor remove 18 cameras today after pausing its Flock program. During Monday’s city commission meeting, one resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store the data and who can access it. Flock, the company behind the cameras, said the agency using the system controls the data, not Flock. The company also said that data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when. Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." While the state’s order applies only to cameras on state highways, Port St. Lucie is taking its own steps by removing the 18 cameras from city streets. The city’s decision reflects ongoing concerns about privacy and surveillance technology. Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after being found floating in a pond on his family’s property, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. The child was playing outside in the yard along Darling Street with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he slipped out of sight for a brief period. When the child’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began searching for him and found him in a pond on the property. The family immediately rushed the toddler to Cleveland Clinic South, where medical staff performed lifesaving efforts. Despite their attempts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators the child was out of their sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone present at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the tragedy. The investigation remains ongoing.

For some people, Common Ground Community Development is a place to learn music or explore the arts. For others, it's a business networking hub, a source of emotional support or even a second home. The Miami Dolphins confirmed earlier this week that running back De'Von Achane tore his ACL on Sunday and will miss the rest of the season.Achane was injured just five plays into Sunday's game against the Kansas City Chiefs, leaving the game after an uncomfortable tackle.Head coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday that Achane has maintained a positive attitude but acknowledged the road ahead will not be easy."As far as how he's doing, he's had a great attitude. I'm sure he's going to have some tough moments," Hafley said. Hopefully that will really help I'll make our defense more dynamic," Spoelstra said.Spoelstra said having both players on the floor at the same time opens up more opportunities defensively."It'll allow them each to make more plays, defensive plays in the paint, blocks, deflections, stops," Spoelstra said.Adebayo and Antetokounmpo both said they plan to push each other in practice to elevate the team's defense."We're a fast team, but not only are we fast, we're switchable, we talk, we communicate, everybody can guard their yard. And that's one through five and from that standpoint, I feel like we're going to be really good." Adebayo said."Because the defense is mindset and effort and I feel like we have guys around the team that have that," Antetokounmpo said.On the offensive end, players including Davion Mitchell, Pelle Larsson and Klay Thompson got in plenty of shots during practice. Spoelstra said this year the team is turning the page and starting something new.The Heat will continue to practice at Florida Atlantic University throughout the week before heading to Toronto to face the Raptors in a preseason game Saturday.

The 650-acre development plans nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000. P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month, offering an early taste of a community where owners will eventually be able to drive on a circuit and head home overlooking it. The 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road is taking shape on a former orange grove. Plans include multiple driving circuits, trackside homes, a motorsports business park and amenities ranging from a pool to walking trails. The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in two separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. According to an arrest affidavit, 23-year-old Giovanny Barthelemy was driving a silver Toyota Highlander around 8:40 p.m. Tuesday when it collided with a 16-year-old riding an electric motorcycle on Southwest Roma Way near Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at the community clubhouse recorded the crash. The officer wrote that the video shows the SUV turning into the community entrance as the teen crossed in front of it. The teen was thrown from the motorcycle. The affidavit says the SUV then backed up and drove away while the injured teen lay on the ground waving his arms. The teen was taken to Tradition Medical Center and then flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said he broke his left femur and hurt his left ankle, and he was listed in serious but stable condition. See also: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges, enters not guilty plea One witness told police the electric motorcycle had no headlights. Two witnesses said both vehicles were going fast. The SUV's owner, the father of Barthelemy's girlfriend, called 911. He told police Barthelemy said he had hit someone on a bike and then driven home. Officers found Barthelemy at his home on Southwest Ridgecrest Drive. According to the affidavit, after being read his rights, Barthelemy told police he felt and heard the crash and knew right away he had hit a person. He told police he should have stopped but didn't, and said his phone was dead, according to the affidavit. Barthelemy is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries, which is a felony. He was also given a traffic citation. He was released on a $7,500 bond. The second case happened earlier that afternoon. Lucie officer clocked a silver Toyota going 85 mph in a 40-mph zone, according to an arrest affidavit. The officer turned around and tried to stop the car. The affidavit says the driver went over a concrete median into the opposite lanes, ran a red light, and hit a traffic sign at Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street before getting on northbound Interstate 95. The officer turned off his lights and siren but kept the car in sight. Police said the car later broke down on the side of I-95. Officers said the driver, 19-year-old Christian Johnson, got out and ran toward the back of the car. Lucie detective, a Florida Highway Patrol trooper, and the officer surrounded the car, and Johnson was taken into custody. According to the affidavit, Johnson's license had been suspended three times in St. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving and driving with a suspended or revoked license. All three charges are misdemeanors. He was released on a $12,500 bond. In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

Investigators said the teen had cognitive and developmental limitations that affected how she communicated. Police ended their initial detailed questioning so a specially trained forensic interviewer could speak with her. The teen described multiple alleged assaults in different parts of the home. After Revange was taken into custody, however, he denied the allegations during an interview conducted in Creole, the affidavit said. Revange told investigators he made the earlier statements to appease the teen’s father. Police arrested Revange on Sept. 27 and took him to the St.

Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

The new Jupiter Fire Rescue department is officially in service, taking over all fire and emergency response duties for the town as of 12 a.m., Oct. The historic transition from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue was marked by a ceremony where Fire Chief Darrel Donatto made the first official radio call, declaring the new agency "in service and ready to answer the call."The launch is the culmination of a months-long journey, closely followed by WPTV, from the initial swearing-in of firefighters to the traditional "push-in" ceremony for the new fire engines.WATCH: Jupiter's new fire department officially launch at midnight.At a ceremony held at the Jupiter fire station to commemorate the official start of operations, Chief Donatto addressed the firefighters and the community, acknowledging the significance of the moment."Jupiter Fire Rescue will assume official responsibility for providing fire and emergency services to this community," Donatto said. "We gather here to recognize those who came before us and to reflect on the responsibility that we now inherit and to reaffirm the mission and principles that will guide this department from its very first call."Just before midnight, the chief's voice came over the radio, making the transition official and signaling to dispatchers and surrounding agencies that the new department was operational."Jupiter Chief, thank you to everyone. We look forward to serving together. Jupiter Fire Rescue is in service and ready to answer the call," Donatto announced.For residents, dialing 911 for an emergency will not change. However, calls will now be dispatched to the new municipal department, and a Jupiter Fire Rescue engine and crew will respond. An Okeechobee family is demanding accountability from the school district after they say their 14-year-old daughter, in a desperate attempt to escape relentless bullying, jumped from a school bus window. The family says that after the girl returned home, she attempted to take her own life and was hospitalized for two days in the ICU.WATCH BELOW: Okeechobee family says 14-year-old daughter jumped from school bus to escape bulliesThis family is now sharing their daughter's harrowing story to raise awareness and push for systemic changes to how bullying is handled. Their public plea and a planned protest aim to ensure that no other child has to endure what they say their daughter has gone through.The family of 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a seventh-grader at the Okeechobee Achievement Academy, says her bubbly personality has faded over the last month due to what they describe as escalating bullying by other girls at her school.The situation came to a head in an incident captured in a viral social media video, which WPTV is not showing. The video shows Estrella jumping from the bus window in the school parking lot and running away."She just feared for her life," said Vanessa Sanchez, a family member. "She didn't trust the bus driver to do anything. She didn't trust going out the front or back door, so she jumped out the bus window."What the video doesn't show is what happened next. The family says when Estrella arrived home, she took a handful of medication and left a note saying, "I'm tired of this," in a suicide attempt. Her family found her in time to get her life-saving medical help. She is now recovering in a different hospital."Her mental state over the past month has been degraded," Sanchez said.The Okeechobee County School District released a statement acknowledging the incident, saying in part, "Every student deserves to feel safe, and we take reports of bullying seriously." The district confirmed it is investigating but stated that federal law limits its ability to comment on individual students.Estrella's family says this was not the first time they reported the bullying to the school and that they will not be sending her back. They are now focused on demanding change."I want them to change their bullying policies, and take it more serious," Sanchez said.The family and other concerned parents are planning a peaceful protest outside the school board building on Oct. 5, hoping their daughter's story will be a catalyst for action. "To the parents, talk to their children about bullying," said Estela Meras, another family member. It's not okay."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in two separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. In the first case, police said 23-year-old Giovanni Barthelemy hit a teenager riding an e-bike Wednesday near Southwest Roma Way and Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at a community entrance recorded the crash. Police said the video shows the driver trying to turn into the community, hitting the teen, then making a U-turn and driving away. Police said the driver did not call 911 or stop to help. The teen was badly hurt and taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital . Police said the car's owner later called 911 after the car came back home damaged. Police said the owner was not driving. Investigators then identified Barthelemy as the driver. Barthelemy is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries. He was released on a $7,500 bond. See also: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges, enters not guilty plea The second case began Tuesday, when officers with the department's Traffic Unit tried to pull over a car near Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street. Police said the driver took off and hit a traffic sign while getting away. Officers later found the car on Interstate 95 and arrested 19-year-old Christian Johnson. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving, and driving with a suspended or revoked license. He was released on a $12,500 bond. In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .
