Gustav Forsling hammered a shot past Brandon Bussi with 4.3 seconds left in overtime to lift the Florida Panthers past the reigning Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes 1-0 in Tuesday's season opener for both teams.On a night when the defenses and goaltenders had the edge, it was a blue-liner who provided the winning play to end a matchup of the last two teams to win the Cup.The Panthers had their final chance with the game seemingly headed to a shootout as Carter Verhaeghe brought the puck into the zone with under 10 seconds left. But Verhaeghe sent the puck back toward Forsling, who fired a one-timer from near the blue line that zipped past Bussi's glove side to end it.That spoiled the end of a three-month celebration for the Hurricanes since beating Vegas in June to cap a 16-3 march to the franchise's second Cup. The final piece was the players gathering at the blue line and tapping their sticks as a championship banner rose to the rafters.That moment came against the Panthers, who reached the Stanley Cup Final for three straight years and won it all in 2024 and 2025. They had twice eliminated the Hurricanes in the Eastern Conference Final in their run, though injuries derailed last year.Getting captain Aleksander Barkov back from that lengthy injury list was one of several reasons to expect the Panthers to jump right back into contention, along with Panthers star Matthew Tkachuk welcoming brother Brady as an offseason addition. There was also the change by bringing in Jacob Markstrom to take over the crease anchored by Sergei Bobrovsky during those title runs.And for much of this one, it was up to Markstrom and Bussi to hold up in net, including against multiple one-on-one quality chances and a combined 13 power plays in regulation.Markstrom finished with 15 saves while Bussi — who posted a shutout in Carolina's Cup-clinching win against Vegas — made 19 saves before giving up the last blast.Panthers: Florida heads west to face the San Jose Sharks on Thursday.Hurricanes: Carolina hosts the Washington Capitals on Friday night.

A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who is remembered by loved ones for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Investigators say Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and began searching. They later found him in a pond on the property Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. One relative, Virginia Maldonado, said she hopes people remember Pablo by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. Others told CBS12 News Pablo was deeply loved by a large extended family spanning beyond Florida. According to the sheriff, investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said. A GoFundMe has been established to help Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo's family with expenses following his tragic death. Those who would like to support the family can donate here .

Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party's chances in November.A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults now blame Trump’s policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran.The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies. But Trump — who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout — remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.RELATED STORY | Fed raises rates despite pressure from Trump to cut borrowing costs“I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Bradford, Pennsylvania, who describes himself as a Republican.“Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He’s not really done what I was hoping he would," said Gault. "He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that.”Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps comingOver the last few months, Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas. adults now say they are “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July. About half are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.Prices are "extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel,” said Pedro Sanchez, 52, of Perris, California, who voted for Trump and works in law enforcement. “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”Trump’s current approval on the economy is a 14 percentage point drop from March 2025, just after he took office for the second time. His struggles on the issue mark a significant departure from his first term, when the economy was often a point of strength.Trump spent much of the 2024 campaign hammering President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats, on inflation and promising to lower prices. Now, there's widespread disappointment with his performance. About 7 in 10 Americans say Trump’s handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected." That includes roughly half of Republicans, who are also broadly concerned about being able to afford groceries and gas.“Groceries are just like kind of out of control. It seems like everything is going up," said Bethany Lnenicka, 41, who operates a small farm in Fairfax, Iowa. “It's just one thing and the next week it's another thing. And of course your income doesn’t go up.”A political independent who typically votes Republican and has voted for Trump three times, Lnenicka said she had hoped his second term would be more like his first.“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better," she said.About 6 in 10 Republicans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, according to the new poll, up from about half in April.“It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction," agreed Kristen Slaven, 41, a mental health therapist who lives in Gluckstadt, Mississippi, and typically votes Republican. She said Trump is focused on the wrong things.“Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can't feed their family," she said.RELATED STORY | Trump is on tour touting the economy, but Americans seem to be losing confidence in the message“I had hoped that it would be better,” Slaven added.Some Republicans are still willing to cut Trump some slackDespite their frustration, most Republicans, 67%, say factors outside of Trump's control are more to blame for high prices.“I think inflation is a very difficult thing to tackle," said Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter who lives in Green Bay, Wisconsin.Though he would like to see interest rates come down, Naumann, who works in the automotive industry, supports tariffs and the war with Iran, believing it was necessary.Overall, however, most Americans, 69%, continue to say the war has not been worth fighting, up slightly from 64% in July. Only 28% approve of how Trump is handling Iran.Americans are also unhappy with Trump's trade wars. adults approve of how he is handling trade negotiations with other countries, down from about 4 in 10 in March. And 64% say he has “gone too far” on imposing new tariffs on other countries, up from 58% in January.Overall, the picture is not better. Only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling his job as president. And about 6 in 10 say the country as a whole is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.The issue on which Trump maintains relative strength is border security, with about half of Americans saying they approve of his performance.Trump faces more blame than Biden didTrump's low grade on the economy rivals Biden’s 28% approval rating in June 2022, when there was record-high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic.But Americans were less likely to blame Biden in the lead-up to that year's midterm elections, a sharp contrast with the solid majority who hold Trump responsible now. In October 2022, 44% of Americans said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside of his control.Sanchez, a Republican who voted for Trump, blames him, at least in part.“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us. Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy,” he said. “I think with Biden, a lot of the stuff was outside of his control. It was all the COVID and how that affected everything else. I don’t think that there was much that he could have done."He had high hopes for Trump's return. Now, things seem worse than under Biden.

Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

The man accused of killing Minister Akeem Moore made his first appearance in Palm Beach County court Thursday morning.Hugh Earp Milner Jr., 38, faces charges of first-degree murder with a firearm and attempted first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of 31-year-old Moore. Court records also show Milner faces additional charges including a weapon offense and warrant-related charges.The charges stem from an incident on the 500 block of Ontario Place just after midnight Sunday, where police say Milner approached Moore and a passenger who were sitting in a parked car, believing the passenger was mistakenly his ex-girlfriend.At the time, Moore was on a date with his girlfriend when they had returned to her residence. The couple had parked facing eastbound toward the house when Milner approached the vehicle.According to witness statements in the police report, Milner began beating on the front passenger window and moved toward the front of the car. The woman immediately recognized Milner as the ex-boyfriend of her sister. Police say Milner believed it was his ex was in Moore's vehicle.The report states that Milner began shouting "Is this what we are doing now?" before reaching into his waistband, pulling out a black handgun, and pointing it at the vehicle and its occupants.Moore attempted to drive away, putting the vehicle in reverse and rolling down the passenger window to yell "Hey man, hey man this not (the ex-girlfriend)." As Moore reversed, Milner shot the passenger headlight. Moore then tried to drive north on Ontario Place while Milner continued firing at the vehicle.Police found Moore's white Ford Fusion in the parking lot of Fire Station #5 at 700 North Congress Avenue with damage to the passenger headlight and rear window, along with a large amount of blood in the driver's seat. At the initial scene on Ontario Place, investigators recovered four spent shell casings and a single projectile.Moore was transported to St. Mary's Hospital where he was pronounced dead just after 3 a.m. Text messages recovered from Milner's ex-girlfriend's phone, sent late Saturday night, contained threatening language, according to the arrest report.The ex-girlfiend told police she had known Milner for 13 to 14 years and was in fear for Moore's life and her sister's safety because she believed Milner came to the house intending to harm her.After being shot, Moore demonstrated remarkable courage in his final moments, according to West Palm Beach Police chief Tony Araujo."Akeem should be remembered as a hero," Chief Araujo said. "Even after being shot, he acted selflessly and courageously, driving his passenger to safety."Milner, who police say is homeless, initially fled the scene but was quickly tracked using Flock license plate readers as he traveled south into Broward County. The Broward Sheriff's Office located and arrested him with assistance from the real-time intelligence system.The Broward Sheriff's Office located and arrested him with assistance from the real-time intelligence system. He was extradited to Palm Beach County late Wednesday night.Moore's family continues to seek answers as they process their loss. "Whatever justice is, truth, answers … understanding why this happened to such an innocent person," said Malik Brown, Moore's cousin.Milner is being held without bond at the Palm Beach County Jail and is scheduled to return to court on Oct. 30.Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact the West Palm Beach Police Department or Palm Beach County Crime Stoppers at 1-800-458-TIPS.

Dozens of frustrated Delray Beach residents confronted a city-hired consultant at a heated community meeting Thursday night, demanding solutions for systemic failures at the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery, including cases where burial plots were allegedly resold. The emotional meeting was a culmination of months of resident complaints and WPTV investigations into poor conditions, maintenance issues and significant record-keeping errors.WATCH BELOW: Delray Beach residents demand answers over cemetery failuresThe anger and frustration voiced by families underscore the deep personal impact of the cemetery's problems, which have left some unable to locate their loved ones' graves and others, like one woman who spoke to WPTV, discovering the plot she bought 18 years ago was sold to someone else. The city has now tasked an outside firm with creating a plan for immediate and long-term fixes.One by one, residents shared painful and personal stories with Stephen Kuehne of Kuehne Cemetery Consulting."I got six family members that had to be cremated because they couldn’t be buried out there," resident Andre Andrews said passionately. "We're tired!"RELATED: Delray Beach woman searches for missing grandparents' graves Nicole Ivy described the anguish of many families. "We have other people who can’t find their loved ones out there," she said. "Those are our ancestors, and we want to preserve and protect them."The community's demands were clear: a comprehensive audit of all records, competent on-site staff, a citizen oversight board, and for the city to purchase more land for expansion."Get something done, besides just saying 'I'm gonna look into it,'" resident Stanley George said. "You need to get these people some solutions."The record-keeping failures are not abstract problems. For Sandra Owens, the issue is painfully specific. She first shared her story with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache at a "Let's Hear It" community meet-up in July.In 2006, a year after her parents were buried, Owens purchased the plot next to them. But during a visit in 2024, she found a stranger buried in her spot."I went to visit my parents' burial site, and lo and behold, there's some guy buried with the whole plot and everything," Owens said.WATCH: Delray Beach woman's burial plot sold twiceThe city of Delray Beach later attributed the mistake to a cemetery management software error that listed her sold plot as available. The city attorney’s office offered Owens a refund, an adjacent plot, or the option to relocate her mother’s remains at the city's expense.At Thursday's meeting, her message was simple: "All I want from the city of Delray is the plot that I paid for."Consultant Stephen Kuehne acknowledged the residents' pain and pledged a thorough review."It pains me, but cemeteries have these problems," Kuehne said, promising that improving customer communication would be the top priority. "The cemetery and your loved ones, and the people that helped found this community, they should be respected and should be cared for and that’s what I’m here to try to make sure that’s going to happen."Kuehne will conduct a full assessment of the cemetery’s records, maintenance, finances, staffing and capacity. The city manager confirmed the review will take several months, with the consultant scheduled to present an update to the community in December.Despite the promises, some residents, including Owens, remain wary."I'm not sure," she said after the meeting. "I want action — I want resolution. That's all I want."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who is remembered by loved ones for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Investigators say Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and began searching. They later found him in a pond on the property Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. One relative, Virginia Maldonado, said she hopes people remember Pablo by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. Others told CBS12 News Pablo was deeply loved by a large extended family spanning beyond Florida. According to the sheriff, investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said. A GoFundMe has been established to help Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo's family with expenses following his tragic death. Those who would like to support the family can donate here .

The investigation began Sept. 26 after police were notified about allegations involving a teen receiving treatment at Lawnwood Regional Medical Center . According to the affidavit, the teen’s family had taken her to a hospital after she complained of severe abdominal and pelvic pain. During treatment, she disclosed that Revange, who is her father’s cousin, had sexually assaulted her, investigators said. Police said Revange, his wife, the teen and several other relatives lived together in the same Port St. During an interview at the hospital and a subsequent forensic interview at the Children’s Advocacy Center , the teen repeatedly identified Revange as the person who assaulted her, according to the affidavit. Investigators said the teen had cognitive and developmental limitations that affected how she communicated. Police ended their initial detailed questioning so a specially trained forensic interviewer could speak with her. The teen described multiple alleged assaults in different parts of the home. She could not provide exact dates but believed at least one occurred Sept. 23, according to the affidavit. According to the detective, Revange initially denied the allegations but later made statements indicating that what the teen said had happened was true. Police said he admitted during the call to having sexual intercourse with her but claimed he could not remember when it began or when it most recently occurred. After Revange was taken into custody, however, he denied the allegations during an interview conducted in Creole, the affidavit said. Revange told investigators he made the earlier statements to appease the teen’s father. Police arrested Revange on Sept. 27 and took him to the St.

The Palm Beach Zoo is lighting up the holidays once again with the return of Zoo Lights, running from Nov. Tickets are now available for this after-hours holiday experience, and this year promises to be completely different from previous years."This year is going to be totally different," said Mike Terrell, director of wildlife conservation impact at Palm Beach Zoo. On one side of the zoo, we're going to have a lot of the traditional holiday lights, but on this side of the zoo, we're doing something totally different. We're gonna be celebrating the lights of nature."WATCH: A sneak peek at Zoo Lights 2026The new approach focuses on bioluminescence throughout the zoo experience. "There's gonna be bioluminescence everywhere," Terrell said. "There's gonna be glowworms in the trees. There's even gonna be bioluminescence in the water."Beyond the stunning light displays, Zoo Lights offers interactive experiences that have become visitor favorites. "One of the other favorites of people who come to zoo lights is to sit around and make s'mores," Terrell said.The event features numerous free activities throughout the zoo for visitors of all ages. "Along with making the s'mores, we're gonna have free activities all around the zoo for kids and adults alike," Terrell said.This year's Zoo Lights features a unique three-chapter storytelling experience. The journey begins with "The Welcome," featuring traditional holiday festivities including a towering Christmas tree with light shows every 20 minutes, nightly menorah lighting during Hanukkah, and activities with Santa and Mrs. The experience concludes with "The Finale," where bioluminescent pathways wind through the zoo's lush landscape.Regular Zoo Lights nights welcome all ages, with special 21+ nights reserved exclusively for adults. The zoo offers group pricing for parties of 15 or more, with tickets priced at $19.25 per adult and $15.25 per child for groups.The event operates rain or shine, with free parking available steps from the entrance. All tickets are non-refundable and non-transferable. The zoo encourages guests needing accommodations to contact them in advance at 561-547-9453.Tickets can be purchased through the Palm Beach Zoo's official website at palmbeachzoo.org/zoo-lights, where visitors can select their preferred date and view current availability, entry times, and pricing.

The Town of Jupiter officially launched its own fire rescue department at 12:01 a.m. Thursday, marking a historic milestone for the community's emergency services.The Jupiter Fire Rescue Department (JFRD) has assumed full responsibility for fire suppression and emergency medical services throughout the town, operating from three strategically located stations. The new department represents the culmination of more than three years of intensive planning and preparation to build a municipal fire rescue operation from scratch.WATCH: WPTV speaks to Jupiter Fire Rescue Department minutes after official launchJFRD operates from Station 10 at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park, Temporary Station 11 at Abacoa Community Park, and Station 12 at 2197 W. Indiantown Road adjacent to Cinquez Park. The department employs 94 operational personnel, maintaining a minimum of 23 firefighters on duty during each shift to ensure round-the-clock coverage.Beyond emergency response, the town has also taken over fire prevention and inspection services through JFRD's Fire Prevention Division. This includes conducting fire inspections, reviewing building plans, and implementing other fire safety measures throughout Jupiter.Just before midnight, JFRD personnel gathered simultaneously at all three stations for ceremonial flag raisings and bell ceremonies. The traditional bell ceremony honored previous emergency responders while symbolically marking the beginning of JFRD's service to the community. Fire Chief Darrel Donatto officially placed the department in service after reading the department's mission statement and core values.“We are tightly aligned with Palm Beach Gardens Fire Rescue," Donatto said. "Our two cities operate as one fire department with nine stations. That’s a big department and we’re ready.”JFRD operates under the mission statement "Your Life, Our Mission."Jupiter residents calling 911 for fire or medical emergencies will now be served exclusively by Jupiter Fire Rescue Department personnel.

Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

Lucie County Fire District's attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership.Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the fire chief, assistant fire chief and district attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it."That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

The new Jupiter Fire Rescue Department is officially in service, taking over all fire and emergency response duties for the town as of 12 a.m. The historic transition from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue was marked by a ceremony where Fire Chief Darrel Donatto made the first official radio call, declaring the new agency "in service and ready to answer the call."The launch is the culmination of a months-long journey, closely followed by WPTV, from the initial swearing-in of firefighters to the traditional "push-in" ceremony for the new fire engines.WATCH: Jupiter's new fire department officially launch at midnight.At a ceremony at the Jupiter fire station to mark the official start of operations, Chief Donatto addressed firefighters and the community, acknowledging the moment's significance."Jupiter Fire Rescue will assume official responsibility for providing fire and emergency services to this community," Donatto said. "We gather here to recognize those who came before us and to reflect on the responsibility that we now inherit and to reaffirm the mission and principles that will guide this department from its very first call."Just after midnight, the chief's voice came over the radio, making the transition official and signaling to dispatchers and surrounding agencies that the new department was operational."Jupiter Chief, thank you to everyone. The Town of Jupiter officially launched its own fire rescue department at 12:01 a.m. Thursday, marking a historic milestone for the community's emergency services.The Jupiter Fire Rescue Department (JFRD) has assumed full responsibility for fire suppression and emergency medical services throughout the town, operating from three strategically located stations. The new department represents the culmination of more than three years of intensive planning and preparation to build a municipal fire rescue operation from scratch.WATCH: WPTV speaks to Jupiter Fire Rescue Department minutes after official launchJFRD operates from Station 10 at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park, Temporary Station 11 at Abacoa Community Park, and Station 12 at 2197 W. Indiantown Road adjacent to Cinquez Park. The department employs 94 operational personnel, maintaining a minimum of 23 firefighters on duty during each shift to ensure round-the-clock coverage.Beyond emergency response, the town has also taken over fire prevention and inspection services through JFRD's Fire Prevention Division. This includes conducting fire inspections, reviewing building plans, and implementing other fire safety measures throughout Jupiter.Just before midnight, JFRD personnel gathered simultaneously at all three stations for ceremonial flag raisings and bell ceremonies. The traditional bell ceremony honored previous emergency responders while symbolically marking the beginning of JFRD's service to the community. Fire Chief Darrel Donatto officially placed the department in service after reading the department's mission statement and core values.JFRD operates under the mission statement "Your Life, Our Mission."Jupiter residents calling 911 for fire or medical emergencies will now be served exclusively by Jupiter Fire Rescue Department personnel.

An Okeechobee family is demanding accountability from the school district after they say their 14-year-old daughter, in a desperate attempt to escape relentless bullying, jumped from a school bus window. The family says that after the girl returned home, she attempted to take her own life and was hospitalized for two days in the ICU.This family is now sharing their daughter's harrowing story to raise awareness and push for systemic changes to how bullying is handled. Their public plea and a planned protest aim to ensure that no other child has to endure what they say their daughter has gone through.The family of 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a seventh-grader at the Okeechobee Achievement Academy, says her bubbly personality has faded over the last month due to what they describe as escalating bullying by other girls at her school.The situation came to a head in an incident captured in a viral social media video, which WPTV is not showing. The video shows Estrella jumping from the bus window in the school parking lot and running away."She just feared for her life," said Vanessa Sanchez, a family member. "She didn't trust the bus driver to do anything. She didn't trust going out the front or back door, so she jumped out the bus window."What the video doesn't show is what happened next. The family says when Estrella arrived home, she took a handful of medication and left a note saying, "I'm tired of this," in a suicide attempt. Her family found her in time to get her life-saving medical help. She is now recovering in a different hospital."Her mental state over the past month, has been degraded," Sanchez said.The Okeechobee County School District released a statement acknowledging the incident, saying in part, "Every student deserves to feel safe, and we take reports of bullying seriously." The district confirmed it is investigating but stated that federal law limits its ability to comment on individual students.Estrella's family says this was not the first time they reported the bullying to the school and that they will not be sending her back. They are now focused on demanding change."I want them to change their bullying policies, and take it more serious," Sanchez said.The family and other concerned parents are planning a peaceful protest outside the school board building on Oct. 5, hoping their daughter's story will be a catalyst for action. "To the parents, talk to their children about bullying," said Estela Meras, another family member. It's not okay."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Dozens of frustrated Delray Beach residents confronted a city-hired consultant at a heated community meeting Thursday night, demanding solutions for systemic failures at the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery, including cases where burial plots were allegedly resold. The emotional meeting was a culmination of months of resident complaints and WPTV investigations into poor conditions, maintenance issues and significant record-keeping errors.The anger and frustration voiced by families underscore the deep personal impact of the cemetery's problems, which have left some unable to locate their loved ones' graves and others, like one woman who spoke to WPTV, discovering the plot she bought 18 years ago was sold to someone else. The city has now tasked an outside firm with creating a plan for immediate and long-term fixes.One by one, residents shared painful and personal stories with Stephen Kuehne of Kuehne Cemetery Consulting.“I got six family members that had to be cremated because they couldn’t be buried out there,” resident Andre Andrews said passionately. “We’re tired!”RELATED: Delray Beach woman searches for missing grandparents' graves Nicole Ivy described the anguish of many families. “We have other people who can’t find their loved ones out there,” she said. “Those are our ancestors, and we want to preserve and protect them.”The community's demands were clear: a comprehensive audit of all records, competent on-site staff, a citizen oversight board, and for the city to purchase more land for expansion.“Get something done, besides just saying ‘I’m gonna look into it,’” resident Stanley George said. “You need to get these people some solutions.”The record-keeping failures are not abstract problems. For Sandra Owens, the issue is painfully specific. She first shared her story with WPTV's Zitlali Solache at a "Let's Hear It" community meet-up in July.In 2006, a year after her parents were buried, Owens purchased the plot next to them. But during a visit in 2024, she found a stranger buried in her spot."I went to visit my parents' burial site, and lo and behold, there's some guy buried with the whole plot and everything," Owens said.WATCH: Delray Beach woman's burial plot sold twiceThe city of Delray Beach later attributed the mistake to a cemetery management software error that listed her sold plot as available. The city attorney’s office offered Owens a refund, an adjacent plot, or the option to relocate her mother’s remains at the city's expense.At Thursday's meeting, her message was simple: “All I want from the city of Delray is the plot that I paid for.”Consultant Stephen Kuehne acknowledged the residents' pain and pledged a thorough review.“It pains me, but cemeteries have these problems,” Kuehne said, promising that improving customer communication would be the top priority. “The cemetery and your loved ones, and the people that helped found this community, they should be respected and should be cared for and that’s what I’m here to try to make sure that’s going to happen.”Kuehne will conduct a full assessment of the cemetery’s records, maintenance, finances, staffing and capacity. The city manager confirmed the review will take several months, with the consultant scheduled to present an update to the community in December.Despite the promises, some residents, including Owens, remain wary.“I’m not sure," she said after the meeting. "I want action — I want resolution. That’s all I want.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County Fire District’s attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership. Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation. Nearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district’s own leaders. “Since this district’s inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,” St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. “They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves.” Those positions include the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,” Hutchinson said. “We’re all still friends,” Boudrias said. “Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.” Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it. “That’s not a good process,” Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee. “It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district,” Fowler said. “So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that’s a pretty impactful message.” Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: “I’m glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue,” adding he “welcomes any investigation from any agency.” Per Sabol’s resignation, Lee said it’s a “sad day.” “She’s been a tremendous attorney for the district,” Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn’t have much to say until it’s over with “We’ll see what the men and women decide,” Lee told Hussey. “I came up on the labor side, I’ve always fought for our men and women on the line.” Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday’s meeting. “This system is so broken,” one attendee said. They want action,” said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins. As the union’s legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, “I think we might actually,” adding, “The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I’m going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What’s the process?” Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. There is no word yet on when results will be released. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo. According to the sheriff's office, the boy was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and started searching. They found him in a pond on the property. Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two year old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. He said investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.
