hero.headline: Two Port St. Lucie Hit-and-Run Drivers Arrested, Both Out on Bond
hero.body:
Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. One crash left a teenager on an e-bike badly hurt, and the driver is now free on bond while police renew warnings about the consequences of fleeing.

In the first case, police said 23-year-old Giovanni Barthelemy hit a teenager riding an e-bike Wednesday near Southwest Roma Way and Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at a community entrance recorded the crash. Police said the video shows the driver trying to turn into the community, hitting the teen, then making a U-turn and driving away. Police said the driver did not call 911 or stop to help. The teen was badly hurt and taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said the car's owner later called 911 after the car came back home damaged, and police said the owner was not driving. Investigators then identified Barthelemy as the driver. He is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries and was released on a $7,500 bond.

The second case began Tuesday, when officers with the department's Traffic Unit tried to pull over a car near Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street. Police said the driver took off and hit a traffic sign while getting away. Officers later found the car on Interstate 95 and arrested 19-year-old Christian Johnson. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving, and driving with a suspended or revoked license. He was released on a $12,500 bond.

In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns Amid Hazing Arbitration Fight
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol has submitted her 90-day notice of resignation, stepping down as the agency faces a contested arbitration fight with its firefighters union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday, saying her employment agreement requires 90 days notice because it is a 3-year contract. Her last work day will be December 31, 2026. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute.

Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement that the District Attorney is eligible for retirement and that the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters," the statement said.

Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp has said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. "There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp said.

The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation.

Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

hero.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Drowning an Accident
hero.body:
A medical examiner has ruled the death of 23-month-old Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo an accidental drowning, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday, a day after the boy was found in a pond on his family's property in Port Salerno. Deputies said Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing, began searching, and found him in the pond. Family members said the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office.

Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children at the time. He said a fence had once surrounded the pond but had broken down over time and was no longer functional. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. Criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and reviewed the circumstances of the death before the medical examiner's ruling. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. He added that investigators found no signs the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," he said.

Budensiek is urging parents to enroll young children in swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision remains the most important way to prevent drownings. She recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents, along with swim instruction starting at a young age. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

Family members remember Pablo for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Relative Virginia Maldonado said she hopes people remember him by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. A GoFundMe has been established to help the family with expenses following his death.

cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert for part of Stuart after a raccoon captured off South Kanner Highway tested positive for the disease. Health officials outlined the alert zone and urged residents to avoid contact with wildlife.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert Wednesday after a raccoon captured in Stuart tested positive for the disease. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later confirmed positive for rabies, according to the department.

The alert covers an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies is present among wild animals in that area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, and an infected animal may appear healthy or behave unusually friendly or aggressively.

Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Florida Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030. Treatment given after an exposure can prevent the disease. Health officials recommended keeping pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations, keeping pets leashed and under direct supervision, avoiding handling or feeding wild and stray animals, not leaving pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors, preventing bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings, and contacting a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home.

Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211. Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns as Firefighters Vote on Chief's Future
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District attorney Kim Sabol resigned Wednesday, minutes after a tense special fire board meeting exposed a gap in district policy over who investigates complaints against the district's own top leaders. Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to an alleged hazing investigation that has roiled the district for months. Firefighters are now casting ballots in a vote of no confidence against Fire Chief Jeff Lee as the fallout continues.

Nearly a dozen people spoke at Wednesday's special meeting, which board members called to address what they described as a major gap in district policy. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said the district has never had a policy spelling out how complaints against its own leaders, including the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney, should be handled. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy.

The controversy stems from an alleged hazing incident reported earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, were fired as a result. Hutchinson said the incident was "just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun." Boudrias said "we're all still friends" and that there was "no ill intent" involving the victims. Months before the incident became public, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Chief Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the same district officials named in it, which Fowler said was "not a good process."

Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and said he welcomes any investigation from any agency. Of Sabol's resignation, Lee called it a "sad day" and said she "has been a tremendous attorney for the district." On the no-confidence vote, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said, adding "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Retired fire captain Mike Jenkins said people at the meeting "want action," and one attendee said "this system is so broken." As the firefighters union continues its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin, Fowler said the board may have authority to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work, saying she plans to raise the question with the board in a week. Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote against Lee.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man gets probation for hiding gun used in June shooting
cards.teaser: Christopher Williams Jr. pleaded no contest to hiding the firearm used in a June shooting on North 19th Street, while the man accused of pulling the trigger has not been charged.
cards.body:
Christopher Williams Jr., 19, of Fort Pierce, pleaded no contest on Sept. 3 to charges of false statement to law enforcement and tampering with evidence in connection with a shooting on the 500 block of North 19th Street on June 2. Under a plea agreement with the State Attorney's Office, Williams Jr. will serve six months of probation and was ordered to pay court costs. He had faced a maximum penalty of six years in a state prison and a $6,000 fine.

According to court documents in St. Lucie County, Williams Jr. initially told Fort Pierce Police Department officers that he was inside his home during the shooting and was not aware it had happened. Officers were told by a witness that Williams Jr. was given the gun after 18-year-old Ja'Shawn Crosby shot his 17-year-old girlfriend following an altercation. In a second interview with police, Williams Jr. admitted he hid the firearm on the property before Crosby left the scene.

Crosby has not been charged in the shooting. On July 8, the State Attorney's Office declined to pursue an attempted second-degree murder charge against him, saying there was not sufficient evidence to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

The plea deal closes out the case against Williams Jr. over his role in concealing the weapon, while the shooting itself remains without charges filed against the man accused of firing the gun.

hero.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Drowning Accidental
hero.body:
The Martin County Medical Examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy in Port Salerno an accidental drowning. Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in a pond on his family's property near Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the child's parents called 911, calling it one of the most heart wrenching calls deputies can receive.

According to investigators, Pablo was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he slipped out of sight for a short time. When his mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and found him in the pond. Family members told investigators Pablo had been out of sight no more than 10 minutes. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts.

Budensiek said a fence had once stood around the pond but had been trampled down or broken over time, leaving it not functional. Martin County Sheriff's Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and found no indication anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said.

Charlene Lyons, President and CEO of YMCA Treasure Coast, said she was devastated when she heard the news. "I started at the Y as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me," Lyons said. She encouraged the public to contact the YMCA for information about swimming lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer, it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status, it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons said. Information about swimming lessons is available through the YMCA Treasure Coast website. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man, 19, pleads no contest in gun-hiding case tied to June shooting
cards.teaser: Christopher Williams Jr. entered a no contest plea to charges of lying to police and tampering with evidence after hiding a gun used in a June shooting on North 19th Street in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
Christopher Williams Jr., 19, of Fort Pierce, pleaded no contest on Sept. 3 to charges of false statement to law enforcement and tampering with evidence, according to court documents in St. Lucie County. The charges stemmed from a shooting on the 500 block of North 19th Street in Fort Pierce on June 2.

Under a plea agreement with the State Attorney's Office, Williams Jr. will serve six months of probation and was ordered to pay court costs. He had faced a maximum penalty of six years in a state prison and a $6,000 fine.

Fort Pierce Police Department officers said Williams Jr. initially told them he was inside his home during the shooting and was not aware it had happened. A witness told officers that Williams Jr. was given the gun after 18-year-old Ja'Shawn Crosby shot his 17-year-old girlfriend following an altercation. In a second interview with police, Williams Jr. said he hid the firearm on the property before Crosby left the scene.

Crosby has not faced a homicide-related charge in the case. On July 8, the State Attorney's Office declined to pursue an attempted second-degree murder charge against him, citing insufficient evidence to prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol Gives 90-Day Notice
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her 90-day notice Wednesday, announcing her exit as the agency fights its firefighters' union over the firing of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday, saying it was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026."

Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline.

The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp has said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing.

The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. The district has declined further comment while the contractual proceedings are ongoing. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Clerk Testifies Board Relied on Mimms in Avenue D Deal
cards.teaser: City Clerk Linda Cox testified on day three of former city manager Nick Mimms' corruption trial that the Fort Pierce board relied on Mimms for accurate information during the Avenue D land deal.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the corruption trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct tied to a land deal involving vacant lots on Avenue D.

The jury first heard from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. "Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. "Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. Attorneys also showed footage from later meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.

Under cross-examination, defense attorney Donald Murrell argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property, and questioned Cox about whether she raised concerns at the time. "You knew they were city employees," Murrell said. "I did," Cox said. "And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said. "I thought it was a little odd," Cox said. "You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said. "I did not," Cox said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings. "He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said. "Yes," Cox said. "He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said. "Not at the meeting," Cox said. "Ever?" Murrell said. "I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

hero.headline: Rabies Alert Issued in Stuart After Raccoon Tests Positive
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a 60-day rabies alert Wednesday after a raccoon captured in Stuart tested positive for the disease. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later confirmed positive for rabies, according to the department.

The alert covers an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies is present among wild animals in that area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly spread through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, and officials noted an infected animal may appear healthy while behaving unusually friendly or aggressively.

Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030. Treatment given after an exposure can prevent the disease from developing. Officials recommended that residents keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations, keep pets leashed and under direct supervision, avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals, and avoid leaving pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. They also advised preventing bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings, and contacting a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home.

Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211. Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies.

cards.headline: Medical Examiner Rules Port Salerno Toddler's Pond Drowning Accidental
cards.teaser: A medical examiner has ruled the death of 23-month-old Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who drowned in a pond on his family's Port Salerno property Tuesday, an accidental drowning. Martin County's sheriff and a local swim school leader are renewing calls for supervision, pool fencing and swim lessons.
cards.body:
Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, a 23-month-old boy, drowned Tuesday evening in a pond on his family's property along Darling Street in Port Salerno, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The Martin County Medical Examiner has since ruled the death an accidental drowning following an autopsy, Sheriff John Budensiek said Wednesday.

According to the sheriff's office, the boy was outside with family members shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children nearby. The mother and aunt realized the boy was missing, began searching, and found him in the pond. Family members told investigators he had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. He was taken to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital, where he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts.

Budensiek said a fence had once surrounded the pond but had broken down over time and was no longer functional. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two year old did not know how to swim." MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene as part of the review. Budensiek said the investigation found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," he said. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning."

Budensiek encouraged parents to enroll young children in swim lessons, noting the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision remains the most important way to prevent drownings, along with door alarms, locked pool gates and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is equally critical. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to begin lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

hero.headline: Florida's Minimum Wage Hits Final Scheduled Increase to $15 an Hour
hero.body:
Florida's minimum wage rose to $15 an hour this week, marking the fourth and final increase under a schedule approved by voters through a 2020 referendum. The minimum wage for tipped workers also increased, rising to $11.98 an hour. Starting in 2027, the state minimum wage will no longer follow the fixed schedule and will instead be adjusted annually for inflation.

Workers say the new wage still falls short of covering the cost of living. A young man named Neff, speaking on Clematis Street on Wednesday, said the wage increase does not keep pace with rising expenses. "Minimum wage is going up but so is everything going up," he said. "You have to have another hustle, or another job so that way you can create more revenue and income for your family; $15 an hour is not enough." In South Florida, where housing and daily expenses run high, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report found that a $25-an-hour wage is considered livable.

The wage hike is also putting pressure on small business owners who have to cover higher labor costs. John Ries, owner of Hot Pie Pizza in West Palm Beach, said he cannot fully absorb the increase without adjusting his prices. "I have to pass that cost on to the consumer; I cannot absorb a 7% increase in labor," Ries said. He said it is his policy to pay employees above the minimum wage, but rising costs across every part of his business make it difficult to keep prices low for customers.

With the scheduled increases now complete, future adjustments to Florida's minimum wage will depend on inflation rates starting in 2027. Workers like Neff say they will continue relying on multiple jobs or additional income sources to keep up with the cost of living, while business owners like Ries say they will keep watching labor costs as a factor in pricing decisions.

cards.headline: Florida Rolls Out Redesigned Driver's Licenses at Service Centers Statewide
cards.teaser: Florida began issuing new driver's license and identification card designs at service centers statewide on Wednesday, but current license holders do not need to replace their cards right away.
cards.body:
Florida began rolling out redesigned driver's licenses and identification cards at service centers statewide on Wednesday. The new cards feature Florida-themed imagery, including the historic Castillo de San Marcos fort in St. Augustine and the Discovery Space Shuttle.

The redesign also includes smaller details worked into the card's layout. An orange is integrated into the design as the "o" in Florida, and an alligator appears inside the REAL ID star printed in the top-right corner of the new licenses.

Current license holders do not need to replace their existing cards because of the redesign. The state will phase out the old card design over time, meaning both the old and new versions will be in circulation as Floridians renew or replace their licenses through the normal process.

The updated designs are now available at service centers across the state as part of the rollout that started Wednesday.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Clerk Testifies in Nick Mimms Corruption Trial Over Avenue D Land Deal
hero.body:
The corruption trial of former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day Wednesday with testimony from City Clerk Linda Cox about meetings tied to two vacant lots along Avenue D. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.

Cox testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence presented by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for the two lots. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.

Assistant State Attorney Brandon White questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. "Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. "Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" White asked. "Yes," Cox said. Attorneys also showed footage from later meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.

Under cross-examination, defense attorney Donald Murrell argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Murrell asked Cox whether she raised any concerns at the time. "You knew they were city employees," Murrell said. "I did," Cox said. "And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said. "I thought it was a little odd," Cox said. "You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said. "I did not," Cox said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings. "He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said. "Yes," Cox said. "He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said. "Not at the meeting," Cox said. "Ever?" Murrell said. "I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns After Hazing Fallout Meeting
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District attorney Kim Sabol resigned Wednesday, minutes after a contentious special fire board meeting called to address fallout from an alleged hazing investigation. Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the investigation, which examined videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, and three veteran firefighters, Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, were fired as a result.

Nearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which board members said was called to address a major gap in district policy over who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said the district has never had a policy for handling complaints against top officials, including the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said. "They, being those positions, have essentially been able to investigate themselves." In September 2025, months before the hazing videos came to light, Boudrias and Hutchinson had filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials named in it. "That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy.

Firefighters are currently casting ballots in a no-confidence vote on Lee's leadership. "It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and said he "welcomes any investigation from any agency." Of Sabol's resignation, Lee called it a "sad day" and said "she's been a tremendous attorney for the district." On the no-confidence vote, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line."

Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting. "This system is so broken," one attendee said. "Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins. As the union's legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin continues through arbitration, calls are growing for the fire board to bring the three firefighters back to work directly. Asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now, what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote, and results have not yet been released.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Pulls All 18 Flock Cameras From City Streets Over Privacy Concerns
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie city commission voted to have its vendor remove 18 Flock license plate cameras from city streets after pausing the program amid resident objections over surveillance and data access.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie city commission voted to have its vendor remove 18 Flock license plate reader cameras from city streets, after previously pausing the program due to privacy concerns. The move came the same day Florida's Department of Transportation deadline required local agencies statewide to remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way, a mandate that did not apply to city streets or county roads. Because that state order left cameras on local roads up to individual governments, Port St. Lucie's decision to remove all 18 of its city-street cameras goes beyond what the state required.

The cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. Critics in Port St. Lucie raised concerns about how the data collected by the cameras is stored and who is able to access it. During Monday's city commission meeting, one resident told commissioners, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing."

Another resident pushed commissioners to go further, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." Flock, the company that makes the camera system, has said the law enforcement agency using the system controls the data, not Flock itself. The company also said data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search conducted through the system is logged, including who performed the search, why, and when.

The commission's vote directs the vendor to remove all 18 cameras from city streets following the program's pause. The decision reflects ongoing concerns among residents and city officials about privacy and surveillance technology in Port St. Lucie, separate from the statewide highway removal deadline that took effect the same day.

cards.headline: P1 Motor Club's First Racetrack 85% Done on Former St. Lucie Orange Grove
cards.teaser: Members are expected to hit the first track within a month at the 650-acre P1 Motor Club on Okeechobee Road, where entry starts at $192,000 and 68 real estate units have already sold.
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month at its 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County. The property, taking shape on a former orange grove, is planned around nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club style amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues on top of that cost.

Chris Duplessis, P1's director of fun, said the club's three-mile track is about 85% complete, with remaining work limited to finishing guardrail sections while newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on the track visible today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals. Duplessis compared the concept to a high-end golf club, but with race cars instead of golf balls. The club plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service.

Duplessis said P1 already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. Planned garage townhomes will place vehicle space on the ground floor with living areas upstairs, and every unit is designed to overlook the track. P1 also plans trackside residences, and Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, many expected to serve as second or third homes. Only members can buy real estate, with homes quoted at $1.4 million purchased separately from membership. Duplessis said residents could begin moving in within about two years, with the full development expected to take approximately five years to complete.

Construction on the larger 4.5-mile circuit and the real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. That circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself, along with planned karting, rally and drifting areas. P1's partnership with Mercedes will supply a fleet of vehicles for members without their own cars, and Duplessis described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences open to nonmembers. Beginners will get instructors to teach driving fundamentals and track rules before advancing, and members whose skills qualify can join club races. The development's broader plans include a clubhouse with a rooftop bar, a pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes, walking trails and a motorsports business park. Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, said he plans to live on the property himself. He said P1 will use local contractors and workers and expects a busy day to draw about 100 members.

The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Detail How Citizen Tackle Ended Driver's Second Escape Attempt
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police say Leon Kevin Gentle-Coaxum fled two traffic stops and rammed a vehicle before a bystander tackled him during a targeted traffic enforcement operation over the weekend.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce man faces multiple charges after police say he fled two separate traffic stops, rammed a vehicle while trying to escape a second time, and was ultimately stopped when a nearby citizen tackled him as he ran on foot. The Fort Pierce Police Department has now released new details on how the chase unfolded and ended during a targeted traffic enforcement initiative over the weekend.

According to FPPD, officers were conducting the enforcement initiative in the area of Okeechobee Road and Jenkins Road on the 25th at around 4:45 p.m. when they stopped a blue Volkswagen Jetta. Officers identified the driver as Leon Kevin Gentle-Coaxum, 21, and determined he was driving with a suspended license. As an officer approached the vehicle, Gentle-Coaxum suddenly fled the traffic stop. Police say he then drove recklessly, speeding into oncoming traffic and maneuvering around stopped vehicles by using the grass shoulder.

Officers located the vehicle stopped in traffic at South 25th Street and Edwards Road and attempted a second traffic stop, ordering Gentle-Coaxum out of the car. Instead of complying, he tried to flee again by ramming a vehicle in front of him. An officer broke the driver's side window in an effort to stop the car. Gentle-Coaxum then exited through the passenger side and ran on foot.

FPPD says a nearby citizen intervened during the foot chase and tackled Gentle-Coaxum, which allowed officers to take him into custody. Gentle-Coaxum is charged with fleeing and alluding with property damages, hit and run with property damages, operating a vehicle without a valid license, and resisting without violence.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire District Attorney Resigns Amid Hazing Fallout, Chief Faces No-Confidence Vote
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol resigned Wednesday, minutes after a heated special fire board meeting called to address fallout from an alleged hazing investigation. Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation. Her resignation comes as Fire Chief Jeff Lee faces an ongoing no-confidence vote among firefighters in the district.

Nearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which board members said was called to confront a major gap in district policy over who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders. St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said the district has never had a policy for handling complaints against the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney, meaning those officials have effectively been able to investigate themselves. In September 2025, firefighters Doug Boudrias and Jordan Hutchinson filed a complaint against Lee and Sabol, and that complaint was denied by the same district officials named in it. "That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy.

The policy gap traces back to an alleged hazing incident in which a third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters, Boudrias, Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, were fired as a result. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." The union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters is ongoing, and calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. Fowler said the board may have the authority to do that and plans to raise the question with the board in a week. "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back," Fowler said. "I'm going to ask the board in a week from now, what do we want to do? What's the process?"

Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and said he welcomes any investigation from any agency. On Sabol's resignation, Lee called it a "sad day" and said she has "been a tremendous attorney for the district." On the no-confidence vote, Lee said he would wait to comment until it concludes. "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Retired fire captain Mike Jenkins said at the meeting that "everybody is fed up" and "they want action." Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote, and there is no word yet on when results will be released.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Removes 18 Flock License-Plate Cameras From City Streets
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie's city commission voted to remove 18 Flock license-plate cameras from city streets after pausing the program amid resident privacy concerns, going beyond a state deadline that only applied to highway cameras.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie's city commission voted to have its vendor remove 18 Flock license-plate cameras from city streets after pausing the program due to privacy concerns raised by residents. The removal came the same day Florida's Department of Transportation deadline required local agencies to take Flock cameras off state highway rights-of-way. That state mandate did not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving Port St. Lucie free to set its own policy, and the city chose to remove its cameras entirely rather than keep them in place.

The cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. During Monday's city commission meeting, residents pressed officials to take action against the surveillance technology. One resident told commissioners, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing."

Another resident urged commissioners to go further, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." Critics at the meeting raised concerns about how the camera data is stored and who is able to access it. Flock, the company that makes the cameras, has said the law enforcement agency using the system controls the data, not the company itself.

Flock has also said that camera data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search of the system is logged, including who conducted the search, why, and when it happened. Port St. Lucie's decision to remove all 18 cameras from city streets goes beyond what the state required, reflecting the local concerns over privacy and surveillance technology raised directly by residents at the commission meeting.

hero.headline: MCSO Reviews Scene Interviews in Port Salerno Toddler Drowning Death
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office criminal investigators are reviewing scene interviews and the circumstances surrounding the death of 23-month-old Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo, who drowned Tuesday in a pond on his family's property in Port Salerno. The toddler was found unresponsive in the pond near Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive after slipping out of sight while outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m.

According to investigators, Pablo had been playing in the yard with relatives when he went missing for a short time. His mother and aunt realized he was gone and began a frantic search before finding him in the pond. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes.

The family rushed the toddler to Cleveland Clinic South, where medical staff attempted lifesaving efforts. Despite those efforts, Pablo was pronounced dead in the emergency room.

Martin County Sheriff's Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone who was at the scene at the time of the drowning. Investigators continue reviewing the circumstances surrounding the toddler's death.

"We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." hero.headline: 23-Month-Old Boy Drowns in Pond on Family Property in Martin County
hero.body:
A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found floating in a pond on his family's property along Darling Street in Martin County, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The child had been playing outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he slipped out of sight for a brief period.

When the child's mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began searching and found him in the pond on the property. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, where medical staff performed lifesaving efforts, but he was pronounced dead in the emergency room.

Family members told investigators the child was out of their sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff's Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone present at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the death. The investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Body-camera video shows arrest of Port St. Lucie man in father's stabbing
cards.teaser: Cartavion Merritt was arrested after admitting he stabbed his 79-year-old father and wanted to kill him. Newly released body-camera video shows how officers took him into custody outside the home.
cards.body:
Cartavion Jermaine Merritt was charged with attempted second-degree murder and aggravated battery on a person 65 or older after Port St. Lucie police said he called 911 and admitted stabbing his 79-year-old father during a domestic incident Saturday night. Police have now released body-camera video showing how officers responded to the home and took Merritt into custody.

Police said Merritt called 911 about 11:01 p.m. to report a stabbing inside a home in the 11200 block of Northwest Blockbird Drive. He told dispatchers he used two knives to stab the victim in the chest and that he wanted to kill him. Merritt also told dispatchers he and the victim were the only two people inside the home and that he had placed the knives in the kitchen sink.

The newly released body-camera video shows officers arriving in the neighborhood, establishing a perimeter around the home and escorting a man away from the property. Police said Merritt exited the house about eight minutes after his 911 call and was taken into custody without incident. Once officers entered the home, they found the 79-year-old victim with multiple apparent stab wounds to his upper chest. Officers and paramedics provided emergency care before the victim was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital as a trauma alert. He was later reported stable but intubated, according to police.

Investigators said they found two knives in the kitchen sink and blood on bedsheets in a bedroom, where they determined the stabbing took place. Police said Merritt later told detectives that he intended to kill the victim. He faces charges of attempted second-degree murder without premeditation and aggravated battery on a person 65 or older, both classified as domestic-related offenses.

Breeze Airways launched four new nonstop routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport to East Coast destinations this week, with introductory fares starting at $74 one-way.

The expansion gives Treasure Coast residents more convenient travel options to major metropolitan areas in the Northeast without having to connect through larger hub airports.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras from city streets after commission vote
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie removed 18 Flock license-plate cameras from city streets Wednesday after the city commission voted to end its program, going beyond a state mandate that applies only to highway cameras.

The Florida Department of Transportation required local agencies to remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by Wednesday. The state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Port St. Lucie had paused its Flock program before the commission voted to have the vendor remove the 18 cameras.

Residents raised privacy concerns at Monday's city commission meeting. One resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way."

The cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store data and who can access it. Flock said the agency using the system controls the data, not the company. Flock also said data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on sexual battery charges involving 16-year-old relative
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man faces three felony sexual battery counts after a 16-year-old relative with cognitive limitations disclosed repeated assaults during hospital treatment. A recorded call captured him appearing to admit to the abuse before he later recanted.
cards.body:
Jean Emile Revange was arrested after a 16-year-old relative accused him of sexually assaulting her multiple times inside their shared Port St. Lucie home, according to a Port St. Lucie Police Department arrest affidavit. Revange faces three felony counts of sexual battery on a person between the ages of 12 and 17 without physical force likely to cause serious injury.

The investigation began Sept. 26 after police were notified about allegations involving a teen receiving treatment at Lawnwood Regional Medical Center. The teen's family had taken her to the hospital after she complained of severe abdominal and pelvic pain. During treatment, she disclosed that Revange, who is her father's cousin, had sexually assaulted her.

Revange, his wife, the teen and several other relatives lived together in the same Port St. Lucie home. During an interview at the hospital and a subsequent forensic interview at the Children's Advocacy Center, the teen repeatedly identified Revange as the person who assaulted her. The teen had cognitive and developmental limitations that affected how she communicated, according to the affidavit. She described multiple alleged assaults in different parts of the home and could not provide exact dates but believed at least one occurred Sept. 23.

Police arranged a controlled telephone call between the teen's father and Revange. Revange initially denied the allegations but later made statements indicating that what the teen said had happened was true, according to the detective. He admitted during the call to having sexual intercourse with her but claimed he could not remember when it began or when it most recently occurred. After Revange was taken into custody, however, he denied the allegations during an interview conducted in Creole. Revange told investigators he made the earlier statements to appease the teen's father, the affidavit said.

Police arrested Revange on Sept. 27.

cards.body:

Opening statements are expected Tuesday, with the trial expected to last through the end of the week, the State Attorney's Office said.

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement says Mimms gave a local nonprofit non-public information and controlled the language of the bid. Two former city employees, including Mimms' niece, formed the nonprofit.

Mimms is accused of rigging the bid process for the Lincoln Park downtown corridor. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The case centers on allegations that Mimms manipulated the competitive bidding process by providing inside information to the nonprofit and exercising control over bid specifications.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year, adopts $971.6M budget
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.

Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.

Mayor Shannon Martin said the city has balanced growth and fiscal responsibility. The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate to 4.8750 for 11th straight year
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

Mayor Shannon Martin said the city has taken a measured approach to lowering property tax rates while continuing to meet the needs of the growing community. The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.

The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.

hero.headline: Florida Highway Patrol to equip troopers with body cameras for first time
hero.body:
The Florida Highway Patrol is set to equip its troopers with body-worn cameras for the first time, a major technological shift for the agency which has historically relied on dash cameras and microphones. The rollout will begin with select troopers as the agency finalizes its rules and guidelines for the new equipment.

According to the police union representing FHP troopers, the decision was driven by the need to update aging technology rather than a legislative mandate. The contract with the agency's existing technology was expiring, prompting the move to body cameras.

"The contract with their tech was coming up," said William Smith, president of the union's FHP chapter. "Nobody said we had to have it because of immigration or anything else. It's just the direction the patrol had to go in."

The move comes as FHP's role continues to evolve beyond state highways, with troopers increasingly involved in operations from spring break enforcement to assisting with federal immigration efforts. Smith said he believes the cameras will benefit everyone involved in a traffic stop or other encounter.

"It protects the civilian that we stop, or the detainee for immigration, or whatever," Smith said. "Maybe the body camera will bring things to light that we do do, and people can see that we are tasked to do a lot of things that back when I was hired we weren't tasked to do."

Legal experts say the new technology represents a win for accountability and evidence gathering. Dave Aronberg, a defense attorney and former Palm Beach County State Attorney, said video provides objective documentation that protects all parties.

"People lie, but video does not," Aronberg said. "Law enforcement can protect themselves against false accusations by the individual. And it's also good for defense lawyers and prosecutors because there's no better evidence than the video itself."

Aronberg stressed that the policies governing the use of the cameras will be just as important as the devices themselves. He said the agency should require troopers to use the cameras as much as possible to give the public more confidence and protect the troopers.

hero.headline: Driver crashes into patrol vehicle in Indian River County, nearly hits deputy
hero.body:
A driver in Indian River County narrowly missed hitting a deputy before crashing into a patrol vehicle and driving into a ditch, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The incident occurred while deputies were blocking a lane to assist with a vehicle being loaded onto a tow truck.

The sheriff's office said two deputies were positioned to block traffic when the driver sped past, nearly striking one of the deputies. The driver's truck then crashed into the back of a patrol vehicle before continuing forward and ending up in a ditch. The close call highlights ongoing concerns about driver awareness around emergency vehicles and personnel working on roadways.

The driver was transported to a trauma center with non-life-threatening injuries following the crash. No deputies were injured in the incident. Authorities have not filed any criminal charges at this time, though the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash continues.

Authorities used the incident as a reminder to drivers about the importance of slowing down and moving over when they see flashing lights on the roadside. The move over law requires drivers to change lanes when possible or reduce speed when emergency vehicles, tow trucks, or other service vehicles are stopped with their lights activated. These laws are designed to protect law enforcement officers, emergency responders, and other workers who must operate in or near active traffic lanes during roadside emergencies and routine traffic stops.

hero.headline: Former Fort Pierce city manager on trial for bid tampering in Lincoln Park project
hero.body:
Jury selection began Monday for former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms, who is accused of bid tampering and official misconduct tied to the Lincoln Park downtown corridor project.

Opening statements are expected Tuesday, with the trial expected to last through the end of the week, according to the State Attorney's Office. Mimms faces allegations that he rigged the bid process for the Lincoln Park downtown corridor. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement says Mimms gave a local nonprofit non-public information and controlled the language of the bid.

Two former city employees, including Mimms' niece, formed the nonprofit at the center of the investigation. The organization allegedly received confidential information that gave it an unfair advantage in the bidding process. Investigators say Mimms manipulated the bid requirements to favor the nonprofit connected to his family member.

Mimms has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The trial will determine whether the former city manager abused his position to steer city contracts to the organization with ties to his niece and another former municipal employee.

hero.headline: Jury selection resumes in corruption trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms
hero.body:
Jury selection is set to resume Tuesday morning in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who is accused of manipulating a city bidding process to benefit a nonprofit connected to his niece. Prospective jurors were told to return to the St. Lucie County Courthouse by 8:30 a.m., with jury selection set to resume at 9 a.m. Judge Michael Linn said he hopes to seat a jury Tuesday and begin opening statements at 1:30 p.m.

Mimms, 53, has pleaded not guilty to charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. Prosecutors allege Mimms knowingly influenced the competitive bidding process in 2024 involving two city-owned lots at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park neighborhood.

Investigators say Mimms worked to ensure the lots would be leased by Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit connected to his niece, while concealing his alleged conflict of interest. The group planned to turn the vacant lots into a community space with a library, classrooms and space for small businesses. Authorities say the organization received information that other bidders did not have, helping it secure a low-cost, long-term lease from the city. The project was expected to receive funding through a $500,000 grant, but the lots remain vacant.

During jury selection Monday, prosecutor Jonathan Bridges asked prospective jurors whether they could listen to witnesses, review the evidence and decide whether bid tampering occurred. Potential jurors were also asked about their knowledge of Fort Pierce city government and whether they could presume Mimms innocent unless prosecutors prove the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt.

The trial is expected to last up to two weeks. If convicted on both charges, Mimms could face a combined maximum of 20 years in prison and $15,000 in fines.

hero.headline: Driver crashes into patrol vehicle in Indian River County, nearly hits deputy
hero.body:
A driver in Indian River County narrowly missed hitting a deputy before crashing into a patrol vehicle and driving into a ditch, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Two deputies were blocking a lane while a vehicle was being loaded onto a tow truck when the driver sped past, nearly striking one of the deputies, the sheriff's office said. The driver's truck then crashed into the back of a patrol vehicle before continuing into a ditch.

The driver was taken to a trauma center with non-life-threatening injuries. No deputies were injured, and no criminal charges have been filed.

Authorities reminded drivers to slow down and move over when they see flashing lights. Florida's Move Over law requires drivers to change lanes when approaching emergency vehicles, tow trucks, utility vehicles, and other service vehicles stopped on the roadside with flashing lights. When changing lanes is not possible, drivers must slow to a speed 20 miles per hour below the posted limit.

hero.headline: Opening statements begin in trial of former Fort Pierce city manager
hero.body:
Opening statements began Tuesday in the trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms, who faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct involving city-owned properties and a nonprofit linked to his niece.

Prosecutors told jurors they would present emails, witness testimony, and city documents to support their case. They alleged Mimms used his position to influence the bidding process for the development of city-owned properties.

"Mimms carefully, skillfully steered the bid for the development of this property so that it would end up in the hands of two city employees. And one of those employees was Mr. Mimms' niece," prosecutor Bridges said.

Mimms is accused of helping Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit founded by his niece, secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties.

Defense attorney Donald Murrell described Mimms' relationship with his niece as distant.

"The state puts a lot of emphasis on the fact that she is my client's niece, and she is, but she can fairly be called a distant niece if that's at all possible," Murrell said.

The defense argued that Mimms did not conspire to commit the crime.

"If you follow the law, you follow the facts, and we're comfortable at the end of this case you will find that Mr. Mimms is not guilty," Murrell said.

The state also called its first witness. Several city officials, including the mayor, are expected to testify.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves 11th straight property tax rate cut despite rapid growth
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate as part of a $971.6 million budget. The tax cut continues despite more than 60,000 new residents moving to the city since 2020.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning in October as part of the city's $971.6 million budget. The council made the decision during the formal budget adoption on Monday.

The tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services.

Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. The trend of tax relief has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.

"Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," Mayor Shannon Martin said. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."

The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.

The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.
